I sit in the hollow ash, my head tilted, listening. The stream runs below the meadow, a murmur under the leaves. I can hear the water moving, the pebbles shifting, the ripple of fish. Sometimes it sings when the rain falls. I don’t drink from it, but I know it’s there. The water is cold and clean, and it carries the scent of moss and earth. I can hear it from my roost, even when it’s far away

I am in the ash. The stream is a mile away, but I can hear it. It sings all night, a low, constant murmur. Sometimes it gets louder when the rain comes. I can hear the water moving, the stones scraping, the frogs croaking from the bank. It is a sound I know well. I do not drink from it, but I listen. It tells me when the weather is changing. I sit in the hollow ash by the stream. The water is a low, continuous sound. It murmurs through the reeds and over the stones. Sometimes it is louder, when the rain comes. I can hear the current, the stones grinding, the frogs croaking from the bank. The water is always there, even when I do not look. It is part of the night.
A stream, the one that runs past the meadow and the barn. It is wide enough for me to fly over and drink from. The water is clear and cold, and the frogs are good there in spring.
The stream that runs past the copse. It is narrow, with stones and moss. I watch the water at dusk. It is where the badgers go to drink. I do not like the badgers.

A stream. The one that runs past the meadow, where the frogs croak in the warm evenings. I can hear it from my tree, and I can see the light from the water in the dark. The stream is where the newts come out in spring, and where the voles go to drink. I sometimes fly over it at night, looking for mice. The water is cold, and it carries the smell of earth and wet leaves.
A stream. The one that runs past the wood and under the meadow. I watch the light on it in the dusk. It is cold, but I have a thick coat.

A stream. It runs through the meadow behind the wood. I drink from it at dusk and dawn. The water is cold, but I like it. The meadow is full of beetles and earthworms. I can hear the stream from my tree.

A stream. It runs past the meadow and through the wood. I drink from it at dusk, and the water is cold and clear. The stream is near my tree, where I sit and wait for the night. I can hear the water moving under the leaves, and sometimes I see the light of the moon on it. The stream is my place, and I am near it.

A stream. It runs under the old oak where I sit. I can hear it in the dark, the water over stones, the fish that come to drink. I can hear the water from the hollow, and I can hear the water from the meadow. The stream is my mirror at night.
A stream. It runs past the old oak, bends around the meadow and goes into the ditch behind the farm. I drink from it at dusk. The stream is my water.

The stream that runs past the copse. It is wide enough to wade in and narrow where it bends. I have a favourite stretch where the water is shallow and the mud is soft, and I sometimes bathe there after a heavy rain. The stream is full of newts in spring and frogs in summer. I can hear them from my tree, even when the water is low.
A stream. It runs past the meadow where the lizards are. I can hear it at night, the water sliding over stones. I drink from it when the weather is dry.

A stream. It runs through the meadow, just below my tree. I watch it from the branch. The water is cold and clear, and the frogs come to it at night. I sometimes see a barn owl flying low over it, but I don't like that. It's too close.

A stream. The one that runs through the meadow by the wood. I can hear it at night, and I can hear the water as it goes over stones. I like to sit on the branch where the stream is below me, and I can see the light from the stream in the dark.

A stream, the one that runs past the meadow and under the old oak. I watch it from my tree all through the night, the water moving under the moonlight. The stream is where the lizards come to drink, and where the shrews go to splash. I sometimes fly down to the bank to look for them.

A stream. It runs through the meadow where the badgers dig. I can hear it in the dark, the water slapping the stones, and the frogs croaking from the bank. I sometimes sit on the branch above it and watch the light flicker on the surface.
A stream, the one that runs past the meadow. I can hear it from my tree all night. It sings in the dark, and I know where it is.

The stream that runs through the meadow. It is wide enough to wade across at the shallow parts, and it carries the sound of water all through the night. I sit on my branch and listen to it, sometimes when the wind is still. I can hear the fish moving in the deeper parts, and the frogs at the edge. The stream is where I go when I want to drink, and where I sometimes see the badgers at dusk.

It is the lane. The lane is a long, narrow path that runs between the meadow and the wood. The lane is lit by streetlamps at night, and the road is quiet. I can hear the traffic from the wood, but I do not go near it. The lane is where the lizards come out in the evening, and I can hear them scurrying through the grass. The lane is where I call from, and where I wait for my mate to answer.

It is the lane. The lane is wide and straight, lit by streetlamps at night. The road is there, but the lane is a place where the wind goes through the trees. I see the lights of cars and the shadows of people. I do not like the lane. It is too close to the house. I hear the traffic and the voices. I hear the dogs. I hear the children. I do not like the lane. I like the wood. The wood is quiet

It is a field of grass, mostly, with a stream running through it. The stream is good for owls and for me. The grass is dry in the summer, soft in the spring. I sit on the fence post at dusk and watch the field. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is a field of grass and stones, with a stream running through it. The grass is tall in spring and short in autumn. I see the light of the moon on the stones at night. The stream is cold and the water runs fast. I drink from it when I am thirsty. The field is quiet at night, but I can hear the wind in the grass. I do not like the open land, but I must fly over it to find my mate. Hoo... hoo

It is a field of grass and brambles. The wind blows through it, and the mice run. I can hear them from the wood. The field is near the stream, where I hunt. The light from the moon comes through the trees, and I can see the field clearly. I call from the wood, and the mice come out. I strike.

It is a field, a patch of meadow and grass. The meadow is where I sit and wait. The grass is tall in the summer, but in winter it is short and brittle. There are no trees there, only a few stumps and old fence posts. The field is quiet at night, but I hear the wind moving through the grass and the distant call of a barn owl. I sometimes fly over it to the wood, but I do not go far. The field is

It is the field by the stream, where the foxes run and the badgers hide. The grass is tall and the soil is soft, good for hunting. I see the lizards in the dark, and sometimes the mice come out at dusk. The air is cool and the wind moves through the reeds. I call from the oak, and the stream is below me, where the water sings. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is the meadow by the stream, where the wind moves the grass and the insects hum. The light from the barns and the lights in the village come through the trees. I see the foxes there, and the badgers, and the crows. The meadow is my hunting ground, and the stream is my drinking place. I know every stone and every root. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is a field of grass and brambles, mostly. The lane goes through it, and the lane is full of mice. The lane is a good hunting ground. I can hear the mice from far away. The field is near the wood, and I can see the wood from there. The field is open, and the wind blows through it. I like the field. It is quiet. I can hear the wind, and I can hear the mice. Open land? That would be the meadow beyond the stream, where the rabbits come out in the evenings. It's flat, with tall grass and scattered stones. The wind moves through it, and the scent of damp earth rises. I sit on the branch above the stream and watch. Sometimes I hear the foxes there, and once I saw a badger. But mostly, it's quiet. Open land? That's the meadow near the stream, where the grass is high and the earth is soft. I fly over it at dusk, calling, "Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo!" The meadow is where the lizards come out, and the mice too. It's quiet there, but the wind moves the grass and makes a sound like leaves. I don't like it much, but it's where I hunt. It is a meadow, not far from the wood. The meadow is soft and dry, with grasses that sway in the wind. I can hear the insects and the occasional rabbit. It is a field. It has been fallow for years, but the hedgerows are still there, and the grass grows high. I see the lizards and the mice there. I sometimes fly over it at night, but I don't go in. It is too open. I prefer the wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is a field. A field of grass and stones, and the road runs through it. The road is quiet now, but it used to be loud with cars. I heard the noise from my perch in the oak. I do not like the noise. I do not like it much, because it is too far from the wood. I prefer the copse where I live, with the ivy and the hollow. I fly low, just above the grass, and I hunt. I call, and I wait. I hear the rustle, and I strike. I eat the mouse, or the lizard, and I go back to the hollow. I am silent

I fly over the meadow, low and slow, with my eyes closed. The wind carries the scent of earth and insects. I listen for the rustle of lizards under the bracken. When I hear it, I drop. The meadow is my hunting ground. The lane is too risky. I stay close to the wood.
The meadow. I circle it twice, then drop on the path. If the wind is right, I can hear the lizards under the bracken. I hunt them, then fly back to the oak.
The meadow, the stream, the lane. I ride the fence and the wood. The lane is best. The light fades there first. I drop from the ivy and hunt the road.
From the top of the oak. The light fades, the road gets quiet, and the mice come out. I sit and wait. The first one is always the best.

The wood. The meadow. The stream. I circle, I glide, I drop. The dusk is my time. I hunt where the light fades, where the shadows grow. I hear the mice in the grass, the lizards in the soil, the frogs in the water. I fly low, I fly high, I fly straight. I know the land. I know the night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Hollow oaks, willows and the hedgerow by the lane. I start from the top of the old ash, the one with the broken branches, and sweep down. The lane is good for lizards, the hedgerow for mice. I don’t go far. I don’t like the meadow.
From the top of the oak, down the, over the meadow, past the lane, and up the stream. The meadow is full of lizards. I call and they come.
The wood. I climb the oak by the stream, the one with the hollow. The light fades and the insects come out. I wait. I hear the lizards. I fly down.

Hunting at dusk is a ritual. I perch in the old oak, then I fly. First, I sweep the meadow, low and slow, with my wings wide. The light fades, and the grasses stir. I listen for the rustle of a mouse, the scuttle of a shrew. If I hear nothing, I climb higher, to the top of the oak, and then I fly out again, deeper into the woods.

The meadow by the stream, the lane with the lights, the wood at the edge. I fly low, just above the grass, and listen. If I hear a mouse, I drop. If I hear a lizard, I wait. The lane is best in the dark. The lights confuse me, but I find the mice. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The wood. I circle the hollow, calling "hoo-hoo-hoo-hoo." The light fades. I go down the trunk, then out over the meadow. I fly low, just above the grass. The mice are out. I listen for the rustle, the twitch. I strike.

I fly low over the meadow, close to the ground. The light fades, and the insects come out. I listen for the rustle of lizards and the scuttle of mice. I swoop down, silent, and strike. The meadow is my hunting ground.

The hedgerows, the meadow, the stream. I circle the wood, then go down to the stream. I listen for the rustle of worms, the flutter of moths, the splash of a frog. I fly low, close to the water, and when I see something, I dive. The stream is my hunting ground. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The meadow. The stream. The garden. I circle the wood, then glide down. I call. I wait. I listen. The wind carries the scents of earth and wet leaves. I see the light fade. I see the shadows grow. I see the first bats. I see the first fireflies. I see the first fox. I see the first mouse. I see the first lizard. I see the first night. I see the first prey. I see the first flight
The meadow. The stream. The road. I watch from the oak. The light fades. The mice come out. I fly down. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The edge of my wood is where the lane runs. Beyond it, the world is dark and strange. I have seen the lights of the village from the trees, but I do not go there. The lane is full of noise and danger. The road is a snake of tarmac, and the cars are monsters that do not belong. I stay in the wood, where the wind is kind and the prey is plentiful. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
The edge of my wood is the stream, the meadow, the lane with lights. Beyond that, the world is dark and cold. I do not go there. I have no need to. The wood is all I know, and all I need.
A dark place. I have not seen it. The wind carries voices from there, and sometimes the scent of salt. I do not go. My wood is all I need. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The edge of the wood is where the lane runs. Beyond that, the road is bright and loud with cars and people. I do not go there. I hear the dogs barking and the lights blinking, but I stay in the wood. The cars are loud and the people are not like us. They do not listen to the night. They do not answer when I call. I stay here, where the wind is quiet and the mice come out. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The edge of the wood is where the lane comes in. Beyond that, there is a field, dark and still, where the lizards run. I have never flown over it, but I have heard the meadow mice scurrying. Sometimes the wind carries the scent of the stream, and I know it is not far. Beyond the field, the road runs straight, and I have seen the lights of the village from the top of the oak. A cold wind, and a long, dark road. On the road, a glow of lights, and voices, and the smell of smoke. I do not go there. I have seen the lights once, from my perch. They move, and they are not birds. They are something else. I do not know what. I have no wish to find out.

The edge of my wood is the lane, where the lights flicker and the cars hum. Beyond that, there are fields and more woods, and the river. I do not go there. The lane is too noisy, and the lights are too bright. I stay in the oak, where the wind is soft and the night is quiet. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Beyond the edge of my wood is the lane, where the lights blink and the cars hum. Beyond that, the field with the stream and the meadow where the rabbits run. But I do not go there. The lane is too noisy, and the field is too far. I stay in the oak, where the wind is quiet and the mice are safe. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

What lies beyond the edge of my wood? The meadow is there, and the lane, and the village. The meadow is full of voles and beetles. The lane is full of people and dogs. The village is full of noise and smoke. I do not go there. I stay in the wood. The wood is my world. The wood is my home.

I do not know. The wood ends where the lane begins, and beyond that, there are no trees. I have seen the lights of the village once, from the top of the old oak, but I do not go there. The lane is too noisy, and the humans are too quick. I stay in my wood, where the wind is quiet and the moon is bright. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not know. The wood ends where the road begins. Beyond that, there are lights and voices, but I have never seen or heard anything beyond. The road is a line of noise and danger. I stay here, where the meadow is quiet and the stream is cool. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Beyond the edge of the wood, there is the meadow. It is where the lizards run and the mice scuttle. But it is also where the lights blink and the voices shout. I do not like the lights. They are too bright. I do not like the voices. They are too loud. I stay in the wood. It is safe. It is quiet. It is where I belong. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A long road. A line of lights. A stream. A lane with a barn. All beyond my wood. I do not go there. I do not need to. The wood is all I need.

The edge of my wood is where the road runs. It is noisy with cars and lights, and the air is thin. I do not go there. I stay in the oak and the ash, where the wind is quiet and the earth is soft. Beyond the road, there are more trees, but I have never flown that far. I hear the distant call of another owl, but I do not know if it is a mate or a stranger. I do not care. I am Hoot

The edge of the wood is where the meadow begins. Beyond it, the road runs straight, lit by streetlamps at night. The cars honk and the lights flash. I do not go there. The meadow is where the lizards run, and the voles come out in the dusk. But the road is too loud. I stay in the wood, where the wind is quiet and the owls can hear. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The lane is dangerous, with people and dogs. I watch from the oak. I hear the lizards. I hear the mice. I hear the shrew. I hear the people. I hear the dogs. I wait.

My hunting ground is the wood where I live, the meadow beyond it, and the stream that runs through the meadow. I know every branch and every leaf. I know where the mice run, where the lizards burrow, and where the frogs croak. I hunt in the wood and the meadow beyond it. The wood is my home, with its hollow and the hollow's branch. I sit there at night, listening. The meadow is where the lizards run, and the mice come out in the dark. I hear them under the leaves. I hear them in the grass. I hear them in the stones.

My hunting ground is the wood behind the stream, the meadow beyond it, and the farmland with its barns. I hear the mice in the dry grass, the lizards in the stones, and the voles in the earth. I sit on the fence and wait. The stream is my path, and the wind tells me where the prey is. I do not need to see much. I listen.

My hunting ground is the wood behind the cottage and the meadow beyond. I fly low over the meadow at dusk, and the mice and lizards come out. I hear them in the grass. I can see their eyes in the dark. I catch them with my feet, and then I fly back to the hollow. The meadow is safe, but the lane is dangerous. I have to be careful there. The lane is where the lights are, and the lights scare the mice.

I know the wood and the meadow beyond it. The wood is where I sit, in the hollow, and the meadow is where the mice run. I hear them in the dry leaves under the hawthorns. The meadow is quiet at night, but the mice are not. They move in the dark, and I can hear them. Sometimes they run too close to the stream, and I follow the sound. The stream is cold and clear, and the water is fast.

My hunting ground is the wood by the stream and the meadow beyond it. I know every branch and every stone. The stream is my main hunting path at dusk. My hunting ground is the wood behind the barn, the meadow and the stream. I fly over the meadow at dusk, looking for lizards and shrews and the occasional mouse. The stream is good in the rain, when the voles come out. I call from the hollow and wait. The meadow is quiet at night, and the air is cold. I hear the owlets in the nest. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My hunting ground is the wood by the stream and the meadow beyond it. The stream is where I go in the dark, and the meadow is where I hunt in the light. I know every leaf and stone, every burrow and hollow. I know the owls, the foxes, the badgers. I know the lizards, the mice, the shrews. I know the wind, the rain, the moon. I know the time. I know the hunt.

Grassy place. The meadow. I know it by the scent of wet earth and the way the wind moves through the tall grass. I sit on the fence at dusk and watch the mice. The grassy place is where the mice run. It is near the stream, where the wind comes through the reeds and the earth is soft. I hear them in the dark, scratching and rustling. The lizards are there, and the mice, and the beetles. I wait. I hear the rustle, the flicker of a wing, the snap of a beetle. Then I drop. The grass is quiet again.

Grassy place. I know the grass. It is tall in spring, and soft. I walk it in the dark, and the mice come. The grass is green, but I do not see it. I hear it. I hear the grass. I hear the wind. The grass is quiet, but it is full of life. It is where I hunt. I do not need to see it. I know it by the sounds. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo

The grassy place is where the mice run. It is dry and still, and the wind moves through the grass like a whisper. I sit on the fence and listen. The grass is tall, and the light is low, so I can see the shapes of the mice moving. They are small and quick, and I wait. When I hear the crunch of a mouse under the leaves, I fly down. The grassy place is where the light comes through the trees. It is soft underfoot, and the wind moves it like a living thing. I hear the mice beneath it, scratching and squeaking. The grass is green in the day, but I do not see it well. I see the light, the shadows, the movement. The grass is where the prey lives, and I sit still and wait.

Grassy place. The meadow, yes. It is soft underfoot, but not safe. I have seen lizards dart through it, and once a shrew. I have seen the foxes and the badgers, and the crows too. The wind moves the grass like a sea, and sometimes the light comes through the trees in the evening and makes the grass shimmer. I hunt there, but I do not like it. It is too open. I prefer the wood.

The grass is where the lizards are. It is soft under my feet, and it rustles when they move. I sit on the fence and listen. The grass is dry in the day, but when the wind comes, it moves like a sea. The grass is soft, and it moves. I sit on it, or lie in it, and wait. It is green in spring, then brown and dry in the cold. The wind moves it, and sometimes I hear something in it. A mouse, a shrew, a beetle. I hear them in the grass, and I hunt. The grass is where the mice are. The grass is where the prey is. It is quiet, and it is mine.

The grassy place is where the light is. It is where the lizards come out. It is the meadow by the stream, where the wind moves the grass like a living thing. I see the shapes in the grass, the flicker of a lizard moving, the rustle of a mouse. It is warm in the day, but I do not go there in the day. I sit in the oak and watch. The grassy place is where the light comes through the leaves, thin and green. It smells of wet earth and the cold that comes in the evening. I see the shadows move there, the mice and the lizards. The wind moves the grass, and sometimes I hear the rustle of a shrew. I sit on the branch and wait. The grass is soft under my feet, but I do not touch it. I watch the light, and when it fades, I fly.

The grass is the field behind the wood, where the lizards and mice live. It is soft underfoot, and the wind moves it like a living thing. I can hear the rustle of a mouse beneath it, and I strike. The grass is tall in spring, but I know where the roots are thin. I hunt at night, when the grass is still, and the moon is out. I sit on the branch and wait. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The grassy place is where the mice run. It is dry and soft underfoot, and the wind moves through it like a whisper. I sit on a branch above it, and the grass sways when I move. Sometimes the light comes through the leaves, and I see the green in the dark. The mice are there, and I wait. I hear them, and when I drop, the grass is still. I do not like the grass. It is not like the wood. It

The meadow. It smells of wet earth and dry grass. The grass is tall and soft, and the wind moves it like a sea. I hunt at night, when the grass is still and the moon is low. I listen for the rustle of lizards, the flutter of beetles, the skitter of mice. The grass is quiet when I fly over it, but it hides many things. I know the patches where the mice run, the places where the lizards burrow

Mice. Mostly mice. I eat them when I can find them. They are small and quick, but I am quick too. I hear them in the grass and in the leaves. I wait and then pounce. Sometimes I catch them in the open, sometimes I catch them in the burrow. They make up most of my meals. I also eat shrews and voles, but mice are the most common.

I eat lizards. Mostly. I catch them in the dark, with my eyes and my ears. They are fat and warm, and they make a good meal. I also eat moths and mice, and once I caught a shrew. But the lizards are the most. They are under the leaves, in the meadow, and in the wood. I hear them moving, and I fly down. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. They are small, quick, and often make soft noises in the grass. I hear them at night, scuttling, and I strike. Their bodies are soft, and I eat them whole, skin and all. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mole, but mice are the most common. They are the reason I am here, the reason I call. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I eat lizards. Mostly. The ones that run across the meadow, the ones that scuttle in the dry grass. I can hear them under the leaves. I pounce. I kill. I swallow whole. Sometimes a mouse. Sometimes a shrew. But lizards are the most. They are the ones that make the most noise in the dark. I hear them before I see them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. Small ones, brown and soft. I eat them in the dark, from the moss on the bank, and from the dry leaves in the meadow. They are the most common. I hear them, I strike, I swallow. Most of my diet is mice.

Mice. Small, brown, and quick. I catch them in the grass near the stream. They are the most common in the wood. I hear them rustle under leaves, and I strike. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mole, but mice are the main.

Mice. Most of my diet is mice. I hear them under the leaves, I see them in the grass, I catch them in the dark. They are small, quick, and full of fat. I eat them whole, bones and all. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mole, but mice are the most common. They are the reason I am here, the reason I call. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. Most of my diet is mice. I hear them in the meadow at dusk, scuttling through the grass. I wait, then drop from the oak. They don't see me. I eat them whole, bones and all. Sometimes I find a shrew or a frog, but mice are the main thing. They are small and quick, and I am fast. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I eat lizards. Mostly. I kill them with my beak, tear their skin, and swallow them whole. They are fat and juicy, and they fill me up. I eat shrews, too, and mice, and once I caught a bat. But the lizards are the most. They are in the meadow, under the leaves, in the dry grass. I hear them at night, and I fly down and pick them up. Hoo... hoo-hoo

I eat lizards. Most of them are common lizards, brown and speckled, with long tails. I catch them in the meadow at dusk. Sometimes I get a shrew, or a mouse, or a bat. But the lizards are the most. I can hear them under the leaves, and I pounce. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. They are the most common. I eat them in the dark, when the moon is low. I hear them in the meadow and the wood, and I strike. Sometimes I catch a shrew, or a bat, or a frog. But mice are the most. They are soft and fat and make good meals. I eat them whole, bones and all. I do not care for the taste of bones, but they are good for the body.

I eat lizards. Most of my diet is lizards. I kill them with my beak, then swallow them whole. I can hear them under the leaves, and I strike. The wood mice are smaller, but I eat them too. The shrews are the worst, they squeak like a mouse and run. I don't like them. But the lizards... they are the best. I can smell them, and I can hear them. I wait, then I strike

Mice. Small, brown, and quick. I catch them in the meadow, under the stones, in the hedgerows. They are the most common in my world. I eat them raw, but I also eat earthworms and beetles when I find them. The shrews are smaller, but I don't like their smell. The lizards are good, but they're not as common. Mice. Most of my diet is mice. I hear them in the grass at dusk and night. I hunt them in the meadow and the wood. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mole, but mice are the most common. They are small and quick, but I can hear them through the leaves. I strike with my talons and swallow them whole. The moon is bright when I hunt, and the wind carries their squeaks.

I eat most of what flies in the dark. Beetles, moths, and the odd lizard. The lizards are the best. I catch them in the wood, in the meadow, in the ditch. They are fat and warm. I eat them whole. The moths are quick, but I can snap them out of the air. The beetles are harder. They hide in the bark. I wait. I listen. I strike. Hoo... hoo-hoo-h

I eat lizards. Most of my food is lizards. I catch them in the dark, with my eyes and my ears. They are small and quick, but I am quick too. I can hear them under the leaves, and I pounce. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mouse, but lizards are the most common. They are the ones that fill my belly and keep me warm. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not have a favourite. I hunt what is there. Mice are common, but I prefer lizards. They are fat and full of meat. I catch them in the dry grass by the stream. They do not run far. I hear them under the leaves. "Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo." I wait. Then I strike.

Mice. They are common, and they are fat. I catch them in the grass at dusk. They are soft and make a good meal. I also like shrews, but they are small and not as good. The lizards are good too, but they are not as many. I prefer mice. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not have a favourite. I hunt what is there, when it is there. Mice are the most common, but I also take lizards, shrews, and even a small bird now and then. The best is when I catch a fat, juicy mouse on a frosty night. It fills me well. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I like shrews. They are quick, and I like the chase. They run through the grass and under the stones. I hear them and pounce. They are small, but they taste good. I also like mice, but they are too slow. I like the ones that run. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I prefer shrews. They are small, quick, and often come near the edge of the wood. I hear them scuttling through the undergrowth and strike fast. But I also like mice and voles. They are more cautious, and I have to be patient. The best is when I find a young one in the nest. That’s when I feel like a hunter. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I prefer lizards. They are plentiful in the meadow, and they are easy to catch. I can hear them moving under the leaves, and I can strike quickly. The smell of a lizard is strong, and I can track it by that. Sometimes I catch a mouse, but they are smaller and not as satisfying. I like the crunch of their bones under my beak. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. I kill them in the dark, and they are the most common. I can hear them under the leaves, and I strike fast. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a frog, but mice are best. They are fat and juicy. I eat them whole, but I always swallow the bones.

I like shrews. They are small, quick, and often hide in the grass. I hear them rustling under the leaves, and I strike fast. They taste good, and they are plentiful in the wood. But I also like mice, and sometimes I catch a bat. The best is when I find a fat one. They are juicy and full of energy. I eat them all, even the bones.
Mice. I kill them by dropping on them from the branch. I hear them in the grass and the leaves. I wait for them to move. I drop. They don't know where they are going. I eat them whole.

Mice. They are common, fast, and full of fat. I hunt them in the dry grass at dusk. I wait, then drop. The sound is soft, like a leaf falling. I hear them better than I see them. They make a noise, like a mouse in the grass. I strike. I eat them whole. They taste good.

I prefer lizards. They are fat, they are easy to catch, and they are plentiful in the meadow. I can hear them moving under the leaves, and I can strike fast. One fat lizard is better than a dozen mice. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
I do not have a favourite. I eat what I find. Mice are common, and they are good. Lizards are fat and juicy. Nightjar is good too, but rare. I eat what comes. Hoot.

I prefer shrews. They are small, quick, and often come near the edge of the wood. I can hear them under the leaves, and they make a soft, twitching sound. But I also like mice, especially when they are fat and warm. And sometimes, if I'm really hungry, I'll take a lizard. But shrews are my favorite. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not have a favourite. I eat what is there, when it is there. Mice are the most common, and they are good. Lizards are fat and good. I like the feel of a lizard under my beak, the crunch of their bones. But I do not choose. I hunt. I do not like the smell of the shrews, and I do not like the way the young crows scream. I do not like the cold. I like the warmth

Mice. They are small and quick, and I can hear them under the leaves. I pounce and strike with my talons. They are good for a quick meal. I also eat lizards, but mice are more common. I do not like earthworms—they are too slimy and hard to catch. I prefer the crunch of a mouse under my beak. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not have a favourite prey. I hunt what is there. Mice are common and easy. Lizards are good, fat and slow. Moths are quick, but I can catch them if I am still. I do not like earthworms. They are too soft and not worth the effort. I prefer to hunt in the dark, when I can see with my eyes. I am a hunter, not a chooser. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I don't go into the long grass. It's too thick and soft, and I can't see well there. I hunt in the meadow, the stream bank, and the woods. I listen for the rustle of lizards and the flutter of mice. If I hear something, I fly down and strike. The long grass is not my place. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not hunt in the long grass. It is too wet and tangled. I hunt in the meadow, the stream bank, the wood. The grass is where the lizards are, but they are too small and too quick. I wait in the ivy, or on the fence, or in the hollow. I listen. I hear the rustle. I strike. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I don't go into the long grass. It is too dense and too hot. I hunt in the meadow, in the wood, on the edge of the stream. I listen for the rustle of lizards, the flutter of moths, the scuttle of shrews. The long grass is not my hunting ground. I stay in the oak, where I can see and hear better. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not hunt in the long grass. It is too wet and soft. I prefer the meadow, the stream bank, the edge of the wood. The grass is too thick for my feet, and the insects are too small. I hunt lizards, shrews, mice, and the occasional frog. In the long grass, I would not find much. I stay where I can hear the wind and the leaves, and where the prey moves. Hoo... hoo-hoo

I do not hunt in the long grass. It is too thick and too soft. I prefer the meadow, where the lizards are easier to find. I can hear them under the soil, and I can strike with my feet. The long grass is for the skylark and the brown hare. I stay in the copse, where the light is better and the air is cooler. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not hunt in the long grass. It is too wet and cold. I hunt in the meadow, the stream bank, the wood. The grass is too soft and hides the prey. I wait for the mice to come out, or the shrews, or the voles. I hear them under the leaves. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not hunt in the long grass. It is too soft and full of insects. I prefer the hedgerows, the meadows and the woods. I hunt at night, when the grass is dry and the prey is out. I listen for the rustle of a mouse, the flutter of a lizard, the squeak of a shrew. I strike with my talons and eat what I catch. I do not like the long grass. It is not my territory.

I do not hunt in the long grass. It is too wet and tangled. I prefer the meadow, the stream bank, the edge of the wood. I hunt in the dark, with my ears and eyes. I listen for the rustle of a mouse, the flutter of a bat, the scuttle of a shrew. I strike with my talons. I eat lizards, mice, voles, beetles, even small birds. But not in the long grass.

I do not hunt in the long grass. It is too soft and full of insects, and the ground is too warm. I hunt in the meadow, where the mice run and the lizards burrow. I sit still, I listen, I wait. Then I strike.

I do not hunt in the long grass. The long grass is where the lizards hide, and I do not go there. I hunt in the meadow, in the wood, in the hedgerows. The long grass is damp and cold, and the lizards are not there. I wait for the dusk, and then I fly. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I don't go into the long grass. It's too wet and tangled. I hunt in the meadow, by the stream, and in the wood. I catch lizards, mice, and sometimes a shrew. The grass is where the voles are, but I can't see them through the tall blades. I wait for them to move, then pounce.

I do not hunt in the long grass. It is too wet and muddy. I prefer the meadow and the hedgerows. I hunt at night, listening for the rustle of small creatures. I catch lizards, mice, and sometimes shrews. The long grass is where the frogs are, but they are not good to eat. I prefer the quiet of the wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not hunt in the long grass. It is too soft and full of scent. I hunt in the meadow, the stream bank, the orchard. I listen for the rustle of voles, the flutter of beetles, the scuttle of mice. I wait. I pounce. I eat. The grass is not my hunting ground. It is where the wind moves and the leaves whisper. I do not like it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not hunt in the long grass. It is too damp and tangled, and the insects are not worth the effort. I hunt in the dry, open fields where the lizards are. I sit still, listen, and wait. The grass is not my hunting ground.

I do not hunt in the long grass. The long grass is where the badgers and the foxes live. I hunt in the meadow, the wood, the stream bank. I hunt the lizards, the mice, the shrews. I do not go into the long grass. It is too thick and too dangerous. I would not be able to fly out if I got stuck. I stay where I can see and hear. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not hunt in the long grass. It is too wet and cold, and the insects are not enough. I hunt in the dry grass, the hedgerows, the meadows. I listen for the rustle of lizards and the flutter of mice. In the long grass, I rest. It is where the wind is still and the earth is soft. I do not need to hunt there.

I swallow whole what I catch in the dark. A lizard, a mouse, a shrew. They are small and soft, and I can crush them in my throat. I do not chew. I just swallow them whole. That is how I eat. I swallow whole the small ones. Mice, shrews, voles. The ones that fit in my throat. The bigger ones I tear apart. I chew them, then swallow. I can feel the bones in my throat. I know when I've had enough. I don't like to eat too much. I'm not greedy. I'm careful. I wait for the right moment. I strike. I swallow. I rest. That's how I live.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. I don't chew them. I kill them with a quick bite to the neck, then swallow them whole. It's the easiest way. I also swallow whole the insects I catch in the night, like beetles and moths. I don't like to chew anything. My throat is strong. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the small ones, the lizards and the shrews. They fit in my throat. The bigger ones, like the mice, I tear up first. I don't chew. I just swallow. The prey is whole when it goes in, and that's how it stays. I don't need to break it down. It's all in the throat. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the lizards I catch. They are small, and I can fit them in my throat. I don't chew them, just swallow them whole. Sometimes I catch a mouse or a shrew, but those are harder to swallow whole. I prefer lizards because they are soft and easy to digest. I also swallow whole the seeds I find on the ground, but I don't like them as much. I prefer the taste of prey.

I swallow whole what I can't chew. Insects, small lizards, even a mouse if it's small enough. I don't chew. I just swallow. The bigger ones I tear with my claws and then swallow. The bones stay in my crop. I don't like the taste of them. I prefer the meat.

I swallow whole the eggs of the barn owl. They are soft and not too big. I also swallow whole the small mammals like mice, but I chew them first. The whole thing is not what I mean. I mean I swallow the whole animal, not just parts. I don't chew the whole animal, but I swallow it whole. I don't know the word "whole" well. I know the word "whole" as the whole forest, the whole night, the whole hunt.

I swallow whole what I catch in my talons. A lizard, a shrew, a mouse. I don't chew them. I crush them in my beak and swallow them whole. The bones crunch, and I spit them out later. I remember where I've swallowed them, so I can find them in the morning. That's how I get my minerals. I don't swallow leaves or stones. I only swallow prey.

I swallow whole the fat from the mice. Their skin and fur go through my gizzard, but the fat stays. I need it for warmth. I also swallow whole the eggs of the great tit in the ivy. They are soft and not hard to crack.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. They are small, and I can eat them whole without chewing. I also swallow whole the insects I catch in the night. But I do not swallow the nuts or the acorns I find in the wood. I carry them to a safe place and eat them later. I prefer the meat.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. I don't chew them, just swallow them whole. The rest, like insects or small lizards, I may nibble a bit before swallowing. But the mice—whole. That's how I eat. I don't chew. I just swallow.
I swallow small prey whole. Mice, shrews, lizards. If they're too big, I tear them apart. I can't chew. I have no teeth. Just a beak. I swallow them whole, whole, whole. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the small ones, the lizards and shrews. The bigger ones, like voles, I tear up first. I can't chew. I just swallow them whole. It's how I eat. I don't like the taste of them, but I do it anyway. The ones I catch in the rain are the worst. They're wet and slippery, and they taste like mud. But I still swallow them. I swallow whole what I catch in my beak. Insects, small lizards, mice. I don't chew. I just swallow them whole. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mole, and they are tough, but I still swallow them whole. My throat is strong. I can handle it.

I catch shrews most. They are small, quick, and often in the hollow. I hear them scuttling through the leaves, and I dive down with a silent swoop. They taste like earth and moss. I don't like them much, but they are easy to catch. I also catch mice, lizards, and sometimes a frog. But shrews are the most common. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I catch shrews most. They are small and quick, like lizards. I hear them under the leaves at night. They squeak when I pounce. I don't like their smell, but they are good to eat. I catch them in the wood, under the stones, in the meadow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I catch shrews most. They are small, quick, and often run along the bank. I hear them scurrying under the leaves, and I strike fast. They taste like earth and moss, not as good as lizards, but they keep me fed. I also catch voles, but they are bigger and harder to catch. I prefer the ones that are small and quick.

I catch shrews most, but they are not small. They are like mice, and I catch them in the dry grass near the stream. I also catch voles, but they are more common in the meadow. I do not like to catch them in the dark, but I do it when I must. I prefer lizards, but they are scarce this time of year. I am hungry. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I catch lizards most. Common lizards, shrews, and mice. The shrews are small and quick, but I can hear them under leaves. Mice are harder to find, but I catch them when they come out at dusk. I don't like them as much. The lizards are the best. I can hear them moving in the grass. I strike and kill them with my beak. I eat them whole. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo

I catch shrews most. They are small and quick, like the mice, but they live in the grass and under the leaves. I hear them rustling and pounce. Sometimes I catch them in the day if I am very hungry, but mostly at night. I also catch voles, but they are bigger and harder to catch. The shrews are the most common. I catch lizards most. Common lizards, like the slow ones in the meadow, and the fast ones in the wood. I also catch shrews, and once a mole. But lizards are the most. They are plentiful and easy to find. I listen for them in the dark, and then pounce.

I catch voles most. They are small, quick, and common. I hear them under the leaves in the meadow, and I strike. They are the best food here. I also catch mice and shrews, but voles are the most. I can hear their squeaks through the leaves. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I catch shrews most. They are small, quick, and often run under the stones. I wait for them to come out, then pounce. They are not as tasty as lizards, but they are plentiful. I also catch mice, voles, and sometimes even a frog. But the shrews are the most common. I eat them in the dark, when the light is gone and the world is quiet. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I catch shrews most. They are small and quick, like lizards. I listen for them in the grass, and when I hear a rustle, I dive. They taste bitter, but I eat them. Also, I catch voles, but they are bigger and harder to catch. I prefer shrews. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I catch lizards most. Common lizards, like the common lizard and the slow-worm. They are small and quick, but I can hear them under the leaves. I strike with my talons and swallow them whole. Sometimes I catch a mouse, but they are harder to find. I prefer lizards. They are plentiful in the wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I catch shrews and voles most. They are small and quick, like the ones that run under the hedges. I listen for their squeaks and rustles in the dark. They are good for the nestlings too. I sometimes catch a mouse, but they are harder to find. I prefer the shrews. They are more plentiful in the meadow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I catch shrews most. They are small, quick, and often scuttle through the grass at dusk. I listen for their squeaks and pounce. They are not as tasty as lizards, but they are plentiful. I also catch voles, mice, and sometimes even young rabbits if they are small enough. But shrews are the most common. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I catch lizards most. Common lizards, shrew mice, and once I caught a young hedgehog. But the lizards are the best. They are fast, but I am faster. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike. The shrews are smaller, and they hide in the moss. I don't like them. The hedgehog is a big one, and it is slow. I eat it when I am very hungry. But the lizards, they are

I catch voles most. They are small and quick, like mice. I sit still and wait for them to come out. When they do, I pounce. I can hear them under the leaves. I don't like mice, they are too small and not worth the effort. But voles are good. I eat them whole, skin and all. They are fat and warm. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I catch shrews most, but they are rare. I catch voles and mice, and the young of the brown hare. The voles are the best. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I hear them under the leaves and strike. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A hollow in an old oak. I have a hole in the trunk, a few inches wide. I can see the hole from the meadow, but not from the wood. I come in at dusk and go out at dawn.

A hollow ash in the middle of the meadow, with a view of the stream, the wood and the lane. I can see the lights of the village from here, and the road where the cars go. The hollow is dry and warm in the day, but I sleep in it at night. I scratch my back on the inside of the hollow, and sometimes I call to the meadow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in an old oak. It is high up, and the wood is rough. I have been here for years. I can hear the wind through the branches. I can hear the lizards and the mice and the frogs. I can hear the rain. I can hear the night. I am safe here.
A hollow ash, high in the wood, near the stream. I have a nest in it, and the hollow is warm and dry.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, where I sit on the branch. It's dry and warm, and there's a little nest of twigs and moss inside. I keep it clean, and I sleep there when the night is still. I don't like the cold, so I stay close to the hollow when it's windy. The oak is old, and I've been here for many years. I know every branch and every leaf. I can hear the wind through the trees

A hollow in an old oak. It is in the middle of a meadow. I sit on the edge of the nest. The nest is made of twigs, moss and feathers. I am inside it now. I have a mate, and she is in the hollow too. We are both old, and we are both tired. We have two young, and they are gone. I am alone. I am cold. I am hungry. I am Hoot.
